name: Black Sigatoka
description: Black Sigatoka is a devastating leaf spot disease affecting banana plants. It significantly reduces leaf area, leading to poor fruit filling and premature ripening of fruit during transport.
symptoms: Small reddish-brown specks on the lower surface of the leaf.
Specks elongate into streaks parallel to the leaf veins.
Streaks broaden into elliptical spots with dark brown to black borders and grey centers.
Large areas of leaf tissue die and dry up under severe pressure.
causes: Caused by the ascomycete fungus Mycosphaerella fijiensis.
spreadMethod: Wind-borne ascospores and water-splashed conidia. Wet and warm conditions accelerate the spore germination and spread.
treatment: Apply systemic fungicides (triazoles or strobilurins) in rotation to prevent resistance development.
prevention: Improve drainage, optimize plant spacing for air circulation, perform regular de-leafing of infected leaves, and use disease-resistant cultivars.

name: Cordana Leaf Spot
description: Cordana Leaf Spot is a common fungal disease of banana leaves. While generally less destructive than Sigatoka, it can cause severe defoliation in warm, humid areas with poor management.
symptoms: Large oval or diamond-shaped spots on leaves.
Spots have a prominent bright yellow halo surrounding them.
Concentric dark and light brown rings inside the lesion, resembling a target.
Lesions often merge, causing large sections of the leaf edge to dry out.
causes: Caused by the fungus Cordana musae.
spreadMethod: Spores are spread by wind, rain splashes, and contact with contaminated tools or clothing.
treatment: Foliar application of copper-based fungicides or mancozeb when disease pressure is high.
prevention: Prune excess leaves to decrease humidity in the canopy, remove infected crop residues, and keep fields free of weeds.

name: Healthy Leaf
description: The leaf appears healthy, with a uniform green color and no active signs of fungal or bacterial infection. Continue standard agricultural maintenance.
symptoms: No spots, streaks, or yellowing.
Firm, turgid leaf texture with intact margins.
Uniform light to dark green surface.
prevention: Maintain proper fertilization, irrigation, weed control, and regular observation to keep the plantation healthy.

name: Panama Disease (Fusarium Wilt)
description: Panama Disease is a notorious soil-borne fungal disease that attacks the vascular system of the banana plant, preventing water transport. It is one of the most destructive plant diseases in history.
symptoms: Yellowing of older leaves, starting from the leaf margins.
Leaves collapse at the petiole and hang down, forming a skirt around the pseudostem.
Splitting of the base of the pseudostem.
Reddish-brown discoloration of the internal vascular strands (visible when pseudostem is cut).
causes: Caused by the soil-borne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Foc), particularly Tropical Race 4 (TR4).
spreadMethod: Movement of infested soil, running water, infected planting materials (suckers), and contaminated machinery or tools.
treatment: No chemical cure exists once a plant is infected. Systemic fungicides are ineffective.
prevention: Enforce strict quarantine, use certified disease-free tissue-cultured plantlets, plant resistant varieties (e.g., Cavendish clones resistant to TR4), and disinfect footwear and machinery before entering the farm.

name: Moko Disease
description: Moko is a highly infectious bacterial wilt disease that affects bananas and plantains. It causes rapid wilting and plant death, representing a massive biosecurity threat.
symptoms: Rapid yellowing and wilting of the inner, younger leaves.
The leaf petioles break, and leaves dry up but remain attached.
Young suckers may blacken and wilt rapidly.
Fruit shows internal dry rot and black discoloration; pseudostem exudes bacterial ooze when cut.
causes: Caused by the bacterium Ralstonia solanacearum (Race 2).
spreadMethod: Transmission by insect vectors (bees, wasps) visiting flowers, contaminated pruning tools, root contact, and infected soil water.
treatment: No chemical treatment is available. Infected plants must be eradicated immediately.
prevention: Remove male buds (de-budding) using a forked stick to prevent insect transmission, sterilize tools with 10% formaldehyde or disinfectants between plants, and quarantine/fallow infected spots for at least 6-12 months.

name: Pestalotiopsis Leaf Spot
description: Pestalotiopsis Leaf Spot is an opportunistic fungal infection that typically attacks weak, damaged, or stressed banana leaves, causing localized leaf lesions.
symptoms: Circular to oval necrotic leaf spots with a dark brown margin.
Spots have a light brown to grey center.
Tiny black pinpoints (fruiting bodies called acervuli) visible in the center of mature spots.
Lesions may enlarge and merge on leaf tips under humid conditions.
causes: Caused by the fungus Pestalotiopsis microspora.
spreadMethod: Spores are spread by rain splashes and wind, entering the leaf tissue through wounds or insect punctures.
treatment: Foliar fungicide spray using Mancozeb or Carbendazim if spots cover a significant portion of active leaves.
prevention: Maintain plant vigor through balanced nutrition, prevent physical damage to leaves, control leaf-feeding insects, and remove dead leaves from the ground.

name: Yellow Sigatoka
description: Yellow Sigatoka is a major fungal leaf spot disease of bananas. It causes significant leaf damage, reducing fruit yield and quality.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots or streaks on leaves.
Spots develop grey centers with a dark brown border.
Severe infections can lead to premature leaf death and defoliation.
causes: Caused by the fungus Mycosphaerella musicola.
spreadMethod: Wind-borne ascospores and water-splashed conidia during high humidity and rainfall.
treatment: Foliar fungicide application, rotated to prevent resistance.
prevention: Ensure good drainage, weed control, and target leaf pruning to lower relative humidity.
